title: Learning About Functions Through Learner-Generated Examples https://tipsforteachers.co.uk/research-learning-about-functions-through-learner-generated-examples/ -- original paper: https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.5951/mathteacher.109.2.0104
author: Craig Barton
summary: This Tips for Teachers research summary covers Dinkelman and Cavey's classroom-based study of fourteen learner-generated example (LGE) tasks used to teach and formatively assess functions in an introductory Algebra 2 course. Rather than solving problems teachers hand them, students in LGE tasks are asked to generate their own examples of a mathematical object meeting given conditions, across numerical, graphical, symbolic, and narrative representations. The researchers found students initially defaulted heavily to numerical representations — the most concrete and least demanding format — but that their fluency across the other representations improved as the unit progressed and they got more practice with LGE tasks. Because LGEs require students to construct rather than simply select or execute, the authors argue they surface genuine misconceptions more reliably than conventional worksheets or homework, giving teachers sharper formative-assessment information about exactly where understanding is thin. A secondary but notable finding is that LGE tasks doubled as writing practice: students initially found writing about their own mathematical constructions difficult, but grew more comfortable and precise in expressing mathematical ideas in writing the more they practised the format.
points: Students defaulted heavily to numerical representations of functions when first generating their own examples, revealing a representational gap that graphical, symbolic, and narrative tasks specifically target.

Because LGE tasks require students to construct an example rather than select or execute a procedure, they are argued to reveal genuine misconceptions more reliably than traditional worksheets or homework.
Repeated practice with LGE tasks across a unit improved both students' comfort generating examples and their fluency moving between different representations of the same concept.

LGE tasks functioned as an unplanned but real writing-skills exercise: students initially struggled to write about their own mathematical constructions but grew more proficient in expressing mathematical ideas in writing over time.
The fourteen-task design gives teachers a ready-made, tested set of Algebra 2 function tasks rather than an abstract recommendation, making the approach directly usable in planning.
quotes: This article from The Mathematics Teacher explores the use of learner-generated examples (LGEs) in teaching functions in an introductory Algebra 2 course.
Analysis of student responses reveals that while students initially favored numerical representations, their use of multiple representations improved throughout the unit.
The study demonstrates LGEs' effectiveness as a formative assessment tool, highlighting students' evolving understanding and identifying areas needing further instruction.
The use of LGEs may reveal student misconceptions more effectively than traditional methods like worksheets or homework assignments.

While students may initially struggle with generating their own examples, this process can be valuable for promoting mathematical thinking and discussion. Over time, students may become more comfortable with LGEs and require less coaching.
Using LGEs can help students develop their ability to write about mathematics, which may be a new and challenging skill for some.
